senses.gloss:
Tata, ‘dada,’ is the pet name for ‘father’ in the Rigveda and later. Cf. tāta and pitṛ.
Foot notes viii. 91, 6; ix. 112, 3.
Av. v. 24, 16; taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 5, 5; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, i. 6, 9, 7; in the vocative as a form of address, Av. viii. 4, 77; aitareya brāhmaṇa, v. 14; vii. 15; aitareya Āraṇyaka, i. 3, 3.
Cf. Delbrück, Die indogermanischen Verwandtschaftsnamen, 449.

Tāta, apparently ‘dada's boy,’ an affectionate term of address by a father (cf. tata) to a son, is found in the Brāhmaṇas, occurring in the vocative only. But in the sense of ‘father,’ through confusion with tata, it occurs also as early as the aitareya Āraṇyaka.
Foot notes aitareya brāhmaṇa, vii. 14, 4; Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad, vi. 1, 6; Chāndogya upaniṣad, iv. 4, 2.
i. 3, 3, where tata and tāta are given as variant forms of the address of the child to the father. Little, Grammatical Index, 75, takes tāta to mean ‘father’ primarily, but this seems unlikely.
Cf. Delbrück, Die indogermanischen Verwandtschaftsnamen, 449, 454.

Tatāmaha, ‘grandfather,’ is found in the Atharvaveda.
Foot notes v. 24, 17; viii. 4, 76. It seems to mean literally ‘great father,’ and to be an analogical formation following pitāmaha; Delbrück, op. cit., 473, 474.
